description: We are a passionate multidisciplinary team bridging space science, technology, and creative design. With expertise across software engineering, game dev, AI, and UI/UX media production, we transform complex NASA datasets into intuitive, high-impact digital experiences. We believe that combining technical excellence, storytelling, and human-centered design is the key to solving critical Earth and space challenges.
summary: Field Shift is a bilingual (English and Arabic) web tool that helps agricultural engineers, consultants and agricultural companies choose a crop rotation for a specific farm using NASA Earth observation data. The user finds the farm by place search, their own location or the satellite map, sets a point or draws the boundary, and gets an environmental overview built from NASA POWER climate data and MODIS/Terra NDVI, with ERA5 and USDA soil data as extra context. The user then compares the current rotation with two alternatives: Field Shift scores each one with transparent, adjustable criteria, estimates effective rainfall and indicative irrigation need for every crop season with published FAO methods, lists risks and exports a PDF or CSV decision report. Every value shows its source and its type (observation, model estimate or calculated indicator). Missing data are shown as unavailable, never invented, and the tool does not forecast yield or profit. A separate Educational Missions section lets learners act as a local agricultural engineer, simulate a crop season in five countries with real NASA POWER data and compare experiments. Field Shift turns free, global NASA data into clear evidence for everyday farm planning.
details:
Space Hunters' Project Solution: Field Shift

Choosing which crops to grow, and in what order, is one of the most important decisions on a farm. A good rotation protects the soil, saves water and reduces risk, but the right choice depends on local climate, water and soil, and that evidence is scattered across satellite archives, climate databases, soil surveys and FAO manuals. NASA data are free and global, yet they are rarely used in everyday farm planning because each source needs technical skills to use.

Field Shift closes that gap. It is a free, bilingual (English and Arabic) web tool that turns NASA Earth observation data into clear, comparable evidence for one question: which crop rotation fits this farm, and why? It is built for agricultural engineers, consultants, agricultural companies and decision-makers, and it works on phones and computers with no account or installation.

How Does Our Solution Work

Farm Analysis & Planning guides the user through six steps. Each step opens only after the previous one is complete, so every result rests on validated inputs.

  • Location & Farm Boundary: search for any place in the world, use My location, type coordinates, click the satellite map, or draw the farm boundary as a polygon. The area is calculated on a spherical Earth model, in feddans or hectares.
  • Environmental Overview: 25 years (2001–2025) of NASA POWER monthly climatology for the farm point: air temperature, rainfall, humidity and solar radiation, chosen month by month. A Recent conditions section adds the last 12 months of NASA POWER, MODIS/Terra NDVI vegetation greenness (MOD13Q1, 250 m), ERA5 evapotranspiration and soil moisture, and USDA soil survey data for farms in the United States. Every block has a source panel with provider, dataset, period and resolution.
  • Farm Information & Crops: the user enters the existing rotation and two alternatives from a catalog of ten field crops with published FAO values for water need, growing period and optimum temperature.
  • Scenario Comparison: for every crop season, Field Shift sums the rainfall, converts it to effective rainfall with the FAO formula and subtracts it from the crop's water need to give an indicative irrigation range in mm and m³/ha. It checks each season's temperature against the crop's optimum range and gives each rotation a 0–100 score from four adjustable criteria: lower water need, nitrogen-fixing legumes, crop-family diversity and pest-cycle breaks. Rotations are ranked only when every scenario has complete data.
  • Risks & Trade-offs: the evidence for water, heat and vegetation stress is listed as clear points to consider, without invented probabilities.
  • Decision Summary & Report: the chosen rotation and its indicators are exported as a PDF or CSV report in English or right-to-left Arabic, ready to share with a client, a manager or a farmer.

Educational Missions

A separate learning experience for students and the public. The learner works as a local agricultural engineer in one of five countries (Egypt, India, the United States, Brazil and Australia), chooses a crop, a real past season and irrigation decisions, and watches the season unfold month by month with real NASA POWER data. The simulation uses FAO methods (Blaney–Criddle evapotranspiration, FAO-56 crop coefficients, effective rainfall, a soil water store and the yield-response factor Ky) to show relative yield compared with a fully watered crop. Experiments can be saved and compared side by side.

The project benefits

  • One workflow instead of many sources: climate, vegetation, evapotranspiration and soil data from four providers, requested for the same location and shown together.
  • Indicators professionals already use: effective rainfall and irrigation need per hectare instead of raw satellite variables.
  • Fair comparison: three rotations evaluated with the same data and the same rules, with the reasons behind every score visible.
  • Traceable and honest: every value is labelled as an observation, a model estimate or a calculated indicator, and missing data are shown as unavailable, never invented.
  • Accessible to all: free, English and Arabic, mobile-friendly, no account needed.

Our goal

To make NASA's open Earth data part of everyday agricultural decisions, especially in water-scarce regions such as the Nile Delta, and to help the next generation understand how climate and water shape what farms can grow. Field Shift supports expert judgement; it does not forecast yield or profit and does not replace field measurements or local extension advice.

What makes it creative

  • It connects open NASA data with simple, published FAO calculations in one light tool, between detailed crop models that need expert inputs and raw data portals with no agricultural interpretation.
  • Honesty is a design rule: grid resolution, data gaps and unassessed criteria are stated, and incomplete scenarios are not ranked.
  • The same evidence serves two audiences: professionals planning real farms, and learners exploring real seasons.

Factors we considered

  • NASA POWER and ERA5 describe grid cells tens of kilometres wide, not single fields; NDVI shows greenness, not yield.
  • Soil survey data exist only for the United States; monthly data cannot show short dry spells.
  • Service time-outs and missing values are handled with retries and caching, and reported clearly.
  • Full Arabic right-to-left support, accessibility and layouts from 360 px phones to desktops.

Tools and Technologies Used

Coding languages and frameworks:

  • JavaScript with Next.js 14 and React 18 for the web application.
  • Tailwind CSS 3 for the responsive, bilingual interface.

Maps and visualisation:

  • Leaflet 1.9 for the satellite farm map and boundary drawing; d3-geo, topojson-client and world-atlas for the world map; lucide-react icons.

Data sources:

  • NASA POWER climatology and monthly APIs; MODIS/Terra MOD13Q1 NDVI through the NASA ORNL DAAC subset service.
  • ERA5 reanalysis (Open-Meteo), USDA SSURGO soil survey, OpenStreetMap place search, Esri World Imagery basemap, and FAO crop water references.

Try It

  • Live website: space-hunters-field-shift.vercel.app
